title: Contiguous Array
description: Brute force to optimized: counting 0s and 1s directly versus relabeling as +1/-1 and tracking the earliest index of each running sum.

blocks.text: Given a binary array nums, containing only 0s and 1s, return the maximum length of a contiguous subarray that contains an equal number of 0s and 1s.

blocks.caption: Relabel 0 as -1, then find the longest subarray whose running sum returns to a previously seen value

blocks.text: Given a binary array nums, containing only 0s and 1s, return the maximum length of a contiguous subarray that contains an equal number of 0s and 1s.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the Longest Stretch Where Wins and Losses Cancel Out
blocks.text: Like scanning a long sequence of win and loss results for the longest consecutive stretch where the number of wins exactly matches the number of losses, with nothing left over on either side.

blocks.caption: Scan the results in order, looking for the longest stretch where wins and losses exactly cancel

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["The entire array has one 0 and one 1","an equal count, length 2","Both values appear exactly once each across the full array"],["Answer","2","The whole array itself is the longest, and only, balanced subarray"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["The subarray [0,1] has one 0 and one 1","an equal count, length 2","No length-3 subarray can balance, since the full array has two 0s and only one 1"],["Answer","2","The longest balanced subarray has length 2"]]}

blocks.text: If nums contains only 0s, or only 1s, no subarray can ever balance, since there is nothing of the other value to match against, giving an answer of 0.

Before counting 0s and 1s separately for every subarray, notice "equal number of 0s and 1s" is a relationship between counts of two different values, and relationships like that often simplify dramatically once relabeled as a single running quantity.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: "Equal number of 0s and 1s" becomes a single, familiar quantity if 0 is relabeled as -1: a subarray with equal 0s and 1s then has a sum of exactly 0, since every 1 contributes plus 1 and every relabeled 0 contributes minus 1, and equal counts of each cancel out completely.

Observation 2: A subarray from just after position i through position j sums to 0 exactly when prefix[j] equals prefix[i], the same prefix-sum-difference relationship used throughout every prefix sum problem, just with the target difference being 0 instead of some other value.

Observation 3: To find the longest such subarray, for every prefix sum value, only the earliest index it was ever seen at matters, since pairing the current position with that earliest occurrence always produces the longest possible balanced subarray ending here, compared to pairing with any later occurrence of the same value.

Observation 4: So a hash map from prefix sum value to the first index it was seen at, checked and updated in a single left-to-right pass, finds every candidate balanced subarray's length in O(1) per position, keeping only the longest one seen.

Whenever a problem needs equal counts of two categories within a subarray, relabel one category as -1 and the other as plus 1, turning "equal counts" into "sums to exactly 0", then apply the standard prefix-sum-plus-hash-map technique, tracking the earliest occurrence of each prefix sum when the goal is length, not a count.
This "plus 1, minus 1 relabeling" trick generalizes to any "equal counts of two categories" question, converting it directly into the well-understood "subarray sums to a target" prefix sum framework.
Check every contiguous subarray directly, counting how many 0s and how many 1s it contains, and track the length of the longest one where these two counts are equal.

items: For every possible starting position, extend the subarray one element at a time, maintaining running counts of 0s and 1s seen so far.
Each time the two counts are equal, compare the current subarray's length against the longest one found so far.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: zeros and ones are reset at the start of every new starting position, then updated incrementally as end grows, avoiding a full recount of the subarray at every single length.
The equality check happens immediately after every extension, since a balanced subarray of any length, not just the longest one from a given start, is a valid candidate.
The running best length is only ever updated to a larger value, since the goal is the single longest balanced subarray, not every one that exists.

blocks.text: Every subarray's true counts of 0s and 1s are directly tracked, so the correct longest balanced subarray is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since every start-end pair is directly checked.
Space: O(1) extra beyond the loop variables.

Limitation: checking every subarray directly ignores that "equal counts of 0 and 1" can be reframed as a single running sum reaching a repeated value, letting every candidate's length be found via a single hash map lookup instead of a fresh inner count.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force independently recounts both categories from scratch for every candidate subarray, but "equal counts of 0 and 1" is really just one running value away from being trivial to check: relabel every 0 as -1, and the running sum after any prefix of the array directly encodes the difference between how many 1s and how many 0s have appeared so far. Two positions sharing that exact same running sum value must have an equal number of 1s and 0s in between them, since nothing net was gained or lost across that stretch. The only extra care needed beyond the standard prefix-sum-plus-hash-map technique is remembering the EARLIEST index each sum value was seen at, not every occurrence, since the earliest occurrence paired with the current position always yields the longest possible balanced subarray.

Treat every 0 as -1 and every 1 as plus 1, and maintain a running sum while scanning left to right. Keep a hash map from each sum value to the earliest index it was first reached at, seeding the map with sum 0 at index -1, representing the position just before the array starts. Whenever the current running sum has been seen before, the subarray between that earlier index and the current one is balanced; compare its length against the longest one found so far.
Relabel 0 as -1, maintain a running sum, and track only the earliest index each sum value was first reached at.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Index","Value treated as","Running sum","Already seen at index?","Length if matched","Why"],"rows":[["0","-1 (from 0)","-1","no, first time seeing -1","-","This running sum has never occurred before, so it is recorded but produces no match yet"],["1","+1 (from 1)","0","yes, at index -1, the seeded start","1 - (-1) = 2","The running sum has returned to 0, meaning everything from the very start through here is perfectly balanced"],["2","-1 (from 0)","-1","yes, at index 0","2 - 0 = 2","This running sum was already seen right after index 0, so the subarray between them is balanced, though it ties rather than beats the current best"],["3","+1 (from 1)","0","yes, still at index -1, the seeded start","3 - (-1) = 4","The running sum returns to 0 again, and pairing with the earliest occurrence, still index -1, gives the longest balanced subarray found so far"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass.
Space: O(n), for the hash map of earliest indices.

Relabeling every 0 as -1 and every 1 as plus 1 means a subarray's running sum increases by exactly the count of 1s and decreases by exactly the count of 0s within it, so a running sum of 0 within some range is mathematically identical to that range having an equal number of 0s and 1s. Two positions sharing the exact same running sum value therefore always bound a subarray summing to 0 between them, and using the earliest such position, rather than a later one, guarantees the longest possible such subarray is found, since a wider range between an earlier occurrence and the current position can never be shorter than one bounded by a later occurrence.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Map entry (sum to index)","Why only the earliest index matters"],"rows":[["A sum value's first-seen index","Pairing the current position with this earliest occurrence always yields the maximum possible length for a balanced subarray ending here"],["A sum value's later occurrence","Deliberately never overwritten in the map, since keeping the earliest index is what maximizes length, unlike Subarray Sum Equals K, which needed every occurrence's count instead"]]}

items: The map is seeded with sum 0 mapped to index -1 before the scan begins, representing the position just before the array starts, so a balanced subarray beginning at index 0 itself can still be measured correctly.
Each element is converted to +1 or -1 as it is processed, immediately folded into the running sum, rather than building a separate transformed array first.
The map is only updated with a sum value's index the first time that sum is seen, deliberately never overwriting an earlier, more useful index with a later one.

The running best length is updated by comparing the current index minus the matched earlier index against it, capturing the true length of the subarray strictly between, and including, those two boundary points.

blocks.text: The "plus 1, minus 1 relabeling" trick is the key insight that turns an "equal counts of two categories" question into the standard "subarray sums to a target" prefix sum framework, and tracking only the earliest occurrence of each sum value is what correctly optimizes for length rather than count.

items: Tracking every occurrence's count in the hash map, as in Subarray Sum Equals K, instead of just the earliest index, which is the wrong tool when the goal is maximum length rather than a total count of matching subarrays.
Forgetting to seed the map with sum 0 at index -1 before scanning, which would miss any balanced subarray that starts right at the very beginning of the array.
Overwriting an already-recorded sum's index with a later occurrence, which would shrink the measured length instead of preserving the maximum possible one.

items: Explicitly state the plus 1, minus 1 relabeling trick out loud before writing any code, and contrast it with Subarray Sum Equals K's count-based map to highlight why this problem needs earliest-index tracking instead.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Find the longest subarray with equal counts of two different categories, like 0s and 1s, or positives and negatives" points toward relabeling one category as plus 1 and the other as -1, then finding the longest subarray summing to 0 using a prefix-sum hash map tracking each sum's earliest index.

items: How would this change if you needed the count of balanced subarrays instead of the longest one? Switch the hash map from tracking earliest index to tracking a running count of how many times each sum has been seen, exactly the technique used in Subarray Sum Equals K.

What if there were three categories instead of two, and you needed equal counts of all three? The simple plus 1, minus 1 relabeling no longer works directly with a single running sum; a more elaborate state representation, potentially tracking two independent running differences, would be needed instead.

How would you find the shortest balanced subarray instead of the longest? Track the latest, most recent, occurrence of each sum value instead of the earliest, since pairing with the most recent match minimizes rather than maximizes the resulting length.
Same prefix-sum-plus-hash-map foundation as Subarray Sum Equals K, differing only in what the map tracks, earliest index for maximum length here, versus running count for total count there.
Same "plus 1, minus 1 relabeling to convert a counting condition into a summing condition" trick reusable whenever a problem compares counts of exactly two categories within a range.

Same "track the earliest occurrence to maximize a resulting length" technique as Maximum Size Subarray Sum Equals k, which uses the identical earliest-index map idea for a general target sum instead of specifically 0.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (relabel + prefix sum + earliest-index map): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Relabel 0 as -1 and 1 as plus 1, then find the longest subarray summing to 0 using a prefix-sum hash map tracking each sum's earliest index

Core Idea: Equal counts of 0s and 1s within a subarray is identical to that subarray's relabeled sum equaling 0, and tracking only the earliest index of each sum value maximizes the resulting subarray length
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)

Most Important Observation: An "equal counts of two categories" condition converts directly into a "sum equals zero" condition through simple relabeling, unlocking the standard prefix-sum-plus-hash-map technique
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: 0 becomes -1, 1 stays plus 1; the longest zero-sum stretch is the answer, keeping only the first time each sum is seen
